_comment: Which requirement manifest governs each document that carries `sce:req`,
or why none does. Read by sce-build/tests/every_annotated_document_is_accounted_for.rs;
that test is the schema, because its reader denies unknown fields and a
second JSON-schema file would be a second answer to the same question.
WHY A REGISTRY RATHER THAN AN ATTRIBUTE IN THE DOCUMENT. `sce:req` is
something a document says: this transition satisfies that requirement. Which
manifest governs the document — or that the document is a fixture bound to no
specification at all — is something THIS REPOSITORY decides. A document does
not know it is a fixture; it is one because of how we use it. Spelling that
as an `sce:` attribute would also widen the accepted subset every backend
reads, for a fact no backend needs.
An entry is exactly one of `governed_by` or `fixture`. A document carrying
`sce:req` and named by neither is refused: that is the arrival this file

unresolved.why: ISO 13400-2 spells this id in the clause body while the REQ box on the same page writes `3.DoIP-134`. sce-build/tests/iso13400_requirement_closure.rs asserts the mismatch is REPORTED rather than quietly resolved, so the citation must stay unresolvable. If the manifest ever gains `DoIP-134`, this entry fails — the fixture's subject would have vanished and the test would be asserting nothing.

documents.fixture: Synthetic ids (REQ_ONENTRY, REQ_ONEXIT, REQ_LOG_LEAF, ...) that exercise which syntactic sites carry an annotation and reach the emitted record. They name no specification, so no manifest can govern them.
One synthetic id (REQ_STATE_S0) proving every attachment site reaches the provenance record. It names no specification.

Synthetic ids (REQ_MODE_ACTIVE, REQ_MODE_SAFE, REQ_MODE_OFF) proving `sce:req` on a lookup ROW reaches `LookupEntry::requirements`. Two of the four rows carry a claim and two do not, which is what makes the annotation per-row rather than per-table. They name no specification, so no manifest can govern them.
